caption: Figure 2. One of several control experiments between two Inception models, one of them uses factorization into linear + ReLU layers, the other uses two ReLU layers. After 3 . 86 million operations, the former settles at 76 . 2% , while the latter reaches 77 . 2% top-1 Accuracy on the validation set.
description:
This figure is a line graph comparing the top-1 accuracy of two Inception models over iterations. The models differ in their activation functions: one uses a factorization into linear and ReLU layers, while the other uses two ReLU layers. The graph shows that the model with linear and ReLU layers reaches a top-1 accuracy of 76.2%, while the model with two ReLU layers reaches 77.2%. The linear model starts lower but eventually surpasses the ReLU model in accuracy.

caption: Figure 6. Inception modules after the factorization of the n × n convolutions. In our proposed architecture, we chose n = 7 for the 17 × 17 grid. (The filter sizes are picked using principle 3)
description:
This figure is a diagram illustrating the factorization of n × n convolutions in the Inception architecture for computer vision tasks. It shows the transformation of a standard n × n convolution into a combination of smaller convolutions, specifically 1xn, nx1, and 1x1 convolutions, followed by a pooling operation and a concatenation step. The diagram highlights the use of n = 7 for a 17 × 17 grid, as per the paper's principle 3 for selecting filter sizes. The components include '1x1', '1xn', 'nx1', 'Pool', 'Base', and 'Filter Concat', with arrows indicating the flow of data from the base layer through various convolutions and pooling operations before being concatenated.

caption: Figure 7. Inception modules with expanded the filter bank outputs. This architecture is used on the coarsest ( 8 × 8 ) grids to promote high dimensional representations, as suggested by principle 2 of Section 2. We are using this solution only on the coarsest grid, since that is the place where producing high dimensional sparse representation is the most critical as the ratio of local processing (by 1 × 1 convolutions) is increased compared to the spatial aggregation.

caption: Figure 9. Two alternative ways of reducing the grid size. The solution on the left violates the principle 1 of not introducing an representational bottleneck from Section 2. The version on the right is 3 times more expensive computationally.
description:
Figure type: Diagram showing two methods for reducing grid size in a computer vision architecture.

Description: The figure compares two methods for reducing grid size in a computer vision architecture. The left method uses pooling to reduce the grid size from 17x17x640 to 17x17x320, then applies an inception block, and finally pools again to 35x35x320. The right method uses an inception block to reduce the grid size from 17x17x640 to 35x35x640, then applies pooling to 35x35x320.

caption: Figure 10. Inception module that reduces the grid-size while expands the filter banks. It is both cheap and avoids the representational bottleneck as is suggested by principle 1. The diagram on the right represents the same solution but from the perspective of grid sizes rather than the operations.
description:

The module starts with a base layer, followed by a filter concatenation, and ends with a pooling operation.
